text: Today I'm going to talk about how you can take your coding agents beyond code generation and how API context might be the answer for that.

text: I'm Kamal.

text: And Postman, as you might know, is the end-to-end API platform.

text: So I'm going to be using our real engineering use cases and workflows on top of our coding agent experiences and what we learned from it and how we have been improving the experience and the effectiveness of our coding agents with API context graph.

text: When we think about improving coding agent performance, the first area that we start looking into is documentation.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Documentation is a great place to start.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But as we all know, developers, we hate writing and maintaining documentation.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's an added overhead.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It costs time, and it becomes tricky to go and maintain over time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But if you offload documentation purely to LLMs to author and maintain, research points out that purely LLM-maintained and written documentation tends to degrade exponentially over time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Some sort of human curation is definitely needed to make it more effective.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Skills and MCPs are a really good alternative to look at, but we all know skills and MCPs are only as good as the context that they're provided to.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Agent memory is actually a really good solution for this scenario.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In terms of real-world experiences, most of this knowledge is probably already tribal knowledge in people's heads, and now it's getting translated into agent memory within the coding agent or the harness.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The biggest limitation factor that we see with this is agent memory is still very limited to an individual user, and no standard patterns have now emerged yet in terms of sharing agent memories across your broader teams or across your entire engineering organization.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: While we were trying to solve this problem for the coding agents on the engineering side, our go-to-market teams were also building business agents for go-to-market agents for their end-to-end executive use cases.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So they've been building custom agents that are purpose-built with customer data that is brought in from multiple data sources.

text: And they have done several iterations to streamline all of this unstructured data coming in from all of these data sources into a structured data on top of which these agents operate.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What they have ended up with is a really optimized like RAG plus GraphRAG pipeline that serves as a centralized context layer that makes all of these individual business agents work really well and solve the problem for all of them.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we started looking at how can we learn from this and what can we do to make the coding agent performance really better.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And when we looked at this, what we realized is in a distributed systems and microservices architecture, APIs are the context layer for you.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Complex engineering architecture is often broken down into domains and models.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And each microservice is responsible for owning one single responsibility as per a model or a domain.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And APIs are what defines what that responsibility is.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And API calls between systems is usually how you identify workflows and user journeys that span across multiple systems.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So agents are only as good as the context that they're given.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we set out on a journey to build the best context layer for the agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we went out to start building an API context graph for what Postman's engineering architecture looks like.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The journey started by identifying and cataloging every single microservice that was on production.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then we identified every endpoint that is exposed by each of these REST API services.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then we captured how each and every one of them is implemented right down to the exact line of code.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: where it was implemented.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we also mapped how each and every service talks to each other and how each endpoint connects to each and every other endpoint.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We also tracked how the data goes all the way down across the stack, including databases and caches and all the way down in the entire stack.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We also identified how applications like front-end, CLIs, APIs, how they interact with the whole backend architecture and backend infrastructure.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We gave all of this data and we indexed all of this data using LLM to produce a centralized and effective context graph layer.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But one key principle that we had in mind always was every single data point that landed on the context graph always had to be grounded down in a hard truth.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that hard truth is either a line of code that is implemented in your code base or it could be an exact trace that is coming from a production telemetry.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: With this in place, we set out on a journey to populate our context graph, and this is a snapshot of what our engineering architecture kind of looks like.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So it is some of the very common patterns that you would expect start to emerge.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You start to see a central cluster of core services, of very tightly intertwined
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In intertwined APIs and services that are tightly dependent on each other, you find one or two heavily bloated services that are on the outer edges of these systems.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The ones at the center is typically what you would classify as tier 0 or tier 1 services.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So now that we have the context graph, when we start looking at how do we measure what does it add in terms of improvements to the coding agents?

text: So we took real examples from the Postman git organize from our organization's git repos.

text: We took real PRs that were raised to the GitHub repos.

text: And for each and every one of them, we identified what the developer was trying to do and what the actual outcome was at the end of the PR.

text: We also took important projects and what were the key design decisions and takeaways that were being discussed in those design discussions.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We mapped each and every one of them into an eval, and we mapped what the actual decision that was taken in retrospect as the ground truth that we wanted the evals to conform into.

text: To run the validations, we were able to get the Postman's AI agent connected to the API context graph, and we were able to validate all of these against the Postman AI agent as well.

text: We also took the same context graph and we made it available as a skill and also compared that against the generic coding agent, in this case, Claude Code.

text: If something goes beyond the dashed line, it just did not meet the bar of what a good score should be on that evaluation.

text: So then we bucketed some of the common use cases and scenarios that we see in day-to-day development and where do they fall under.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One key scenario that we always notice is API discovery.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Any developer who is making a change either to the front end or back end, integrating with other systems, what is the right API to call?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And in real-world systems, you probably have hundreds of different APIs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And most likely, you have multiple APIs that probably do the same thing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So in this case, a simplified example that I've taken is what is the right API to call to get the profile name for a particular user.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So in this evaluation, this is a pure search use case, and the results are what you would expect.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: With the context graph, the agents go really well as compared to pure code search, where the agents don't do really well.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And there's a slight deviation between Postman and Claude, but the deviation is not that big enough for us to be diving deeper into.

text: The second use case is where it gets really interesting.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this is what we call API design and redesign scenarios.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So in this scenario, let's take a developer who's building a new feature.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And to build that feature out, they've designed a new API.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And they've designed the schema for the request input.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They have defined the implementation of it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They have tested it out from their side.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then they go integrate it with the product.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And they are happy with the product.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And they are ready to ship.

text: At the last minute, one of the dependencies comes to them and then say, hey, would it be nice if I just had this one additional property that I would like to pass to this API that I would like to use at a later point in time?

text: So the developer is like, maybe we don't have enough time to evaluate all the different ways in which it can be done, what is the right schema to do this?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So they just add this one additional context, which is a freeform JSON object, and they add a todo in the code saying, revisit this and add a schema two weeks later.

text: The feature ships to production.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Everybody's happy.

text: Two weeks later, the developer comes back and finds out that that one particular property, which is supposed to send one attribute, now has 15 attributes.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And it's being passed by one service.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It might be five services.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It might be 10 services.

text: Now the developer has no idea what exactly is the shape in which the request is being passed down to the API, and what are all the different ways in which every single consumer has been passing data down to.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this is what I call like analysis of a shape of input for each and every API and why they are used like that.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this can be hard for a bunch of reasons.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: First, tracking down every single consumer of your API can be impractical in real-world scenarios.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Even if you had service dependencies and service maps, finding out the exact shape of input used by each and every consumer can get really tricky.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Engineers often lack the detail or depth of information in production logs and for privacy reasons it may not even be available at a lot of times.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Even if the shapes are identified, finding out exactly why the consumer decided to pass it down like this is a very, very tricky problem.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But in this scenario, when we took this evaluation and then ran it with the Postman agent, what was surprising was the Postman agent almost got it really well.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: of where exactly each of these APIs were implemented in code, and the context surrounding that code helped the agent understand why the change was done.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And very quickly it was able to figure out exact unique shapes for every consumer that was calling this API, and you could be able to make the changes quite reliably and confidently.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And you can see that the pure code search does not do really well.

speaker: SPEAKER_00

speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this is one scenario where we see the context graph really shine well, and you can see that Postman Agent not only does really well in terms of the quality of the output, but also it's able to do it with almost like half or even one third when compared to your code search.

text: But this is not smooth sailing all the time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Sometimes we see failures.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And in this case, one of the use cases that we threw at it was find out the impact of a change in one particular PR, where it introduced a change to an endpoint, and figure out all the downstream services that are affected by that endpoint.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we started seeing a failure.

text: We see Postman not only scrolling down, but also consuming a lot of tokens while it did that.

speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the context graph is not only important to populate, but it's equally important that you keep it up to date, and any delays in syncing your context graph with the ground truth creates gap in the result.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And if there's a gap in the result, it immediately leads to a loss of trust by the developer, and that translates into lack of usage.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Not only detecting new APIs and new dependencies, detecting removals of APIs and removal of dependencies is equally important and that can also lead to confusions and problems.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So you might think that these use cases may or may not be common to you, but when we went back and retrospected on all the PRs that were raised in the top 10 repos, we noticed that almost 75% of the PRs had some effect on the APIs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So either these changes are introducing a change to the external surface area of an API,
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Or they are introducing an integration of a new API.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And both of them can have really cascading impact downstream.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So these use cases were clear for us to do a before and after comparison with the context graph and without the context graph.

text: It found out interesting insights for us, including cycles of dependencies, which can be really problematic in terms of an incident, risky long-running migrations, which are signals of technical debt, and then single points of failure, which can be really problematic or issues that are waiting to happen, blind spots in telemetry, where stuff that is in the implementation does not reflect in telemetry, and then it came out with clear action items for, hey, this is what your CEO, this is what your CTO, and this is what your staff engineers might need to do.

text: It shortens the time to find the right way to do a particular problem.
